title: How to Keep Track of Follow-Ups at Work
summary: Learn how to keep track of follow-ups at work with 8 simple habits, from a two-list system to a weekly review, so nothing you promised slips through.
body_markdown:
If you've ever wondered how to keep track of follow-ups at work, you know the feeling. You told a client you'd send the deck by Thursday. You asked your head of sales for updated numbers. Someone in a meeting said "let's circle back on pricing next week," and everyone nodded.


Three days later, half of that has quietly disappeared.


Dropped follow-ups rarely come from laziness. They come from volume. Commitments get made in email, Slack, meetings and hallway chats, and none of those places were built to remind you. The fix isn't more willpower. It's a simple system that catches commitments where they're made and puts them somewhere you'll actually look.


Here are eight habits that do that.


## Key takeaways


-


Split follow-ups into two lists: what **you owe** others and what you're **waiting on** from them.


-


Write every follow-up as **who, what and when** , and keep it all in one place.


-


Review the list weekly, and automate capture if your follow-ups mostly live in email and Slack.


## How to keep track of follow-ups at work, step by step


Each habit below takes a few minutes to set up. Start with the first two, then add the rest as they stick.


## 1. Keep two lists, not one


Most people track only what they owe. The other half, what others owe you, is where things really slip. You asked for a contract review, they said "on it," and the request vanishes from your mind as soon as it leaves theirs.


Keep two separate lists:


-


**I owe:** replies, documents, decisions and introductions you've promised.


-


**Waiting on:** anything you've asked someone else for and need back.


The "waiting on" list is especially valuable for leaders. Every project that stalls usually has an unanswered request at the center of it.


## 2. Capture follow-ups the moment they're made


A follow-up is easiest to record in the moment it's created. Ten minutes later, you're in another meeting and it's gone.


Make capture fast. Use one shortcut on your phone or one keyboard command on your laptop that adds to your list. If writing it down takes more than five seconds, you won't do it consistently.


A useful rule: if you say "I'll," "let me" or "I'll get back to you," capture it before the conversation ends.


## 3. Use one source of truth


Sticky notes, starred emails, flagged Slack messages, notes app, the back of a notebook. Each one feels like it's tracking something, but together they guarantee you'll miss things, because you can't check five places every day.


Pick one place where every follow-up lives. A task app, a spreadsheet or a dedicated tool all work (our roundup of the best AI to-do list apps compares a few). What matters is that you trust it enough to stop holding commitments in your head.


This also helps with prioritization. When everything sits in one list, you can see which follow-ups matter most. (If everything feels urgent, our guide on how to prioritize tasks when everything is P0 can help.)


## 4. Write every follow-up as who, what and when


"Follow up with Dana" isn't a follow-up. It's a vague worry.


A useful entry answers three questions:


-


**Who** owns the next move?


-


**What** exactly needs to happen?


-


**When** is it due, or when should you check in?


So instead of "Dana, pricing," write "Dana to send revised pricing for the Acme renewal, check in Wednesday." Now you know exactly what to do when the item comes up.


## 5. Close the loop at the end of every meeting


Meetings are where follow-ups go to die. Everyone leaves with a slightly different memory of who agreed to what.


Spend the last two minutes reading back every action item, with an owner and a date for each. Then send a short recap in writing. The recap does two things: it puts the commitments on record, and it gives you something to search later.


Executives get even more out of this when they walk into each meeting already knowing what's outstanding with those people. A quick look at the "waiting on" list before a one-on-one turns a status check into a real conversation.


## 6. Run a 15-minute weekly follow-up review


Even a great system decays without maintenance. Once a week, block 15 minutes to go through both lists:


1.


Mark anything done as done, so the list stays trustworthy.


2.


Nudge anyone who's overdue.


3.


Re-date anything that slipped for a good reason.


4.


Delete anything that no longer matters.


Friday afternoon works well for this. You close out the week, and Monday starts clean. If you already do a daily morning brief, add your two follow-up lists to it and the weekly review gets much shorter.


## 7. Make nudging easy (and polite)


A lot of follow-ups stall because chasing feels awkward. Make it easier with a few short templates you can paste and tweak:


-


"Quick check on the pricing update. Anything you need from me to get it over the line?"


-


"Bumping this up in case it got buried. Still on track for Friday?"


-


"No rush if this has moved down the list, just let me know so I can plan around it."


Short, friendly nudges get answers. Long, apologetic ones get skimmed.


## 8. Automate the capture


Here's the honest catch with every habit above: they all depend on you noticing each commitment and writing it down. On a busy day, with hundreds of emails and Slack messages, that's where the system breaks.


That's why more leaders now use AI to do the capture for them. Tools that read your email, Slack and meeting notes can spot commitments in both directions, things you promised and things others promised you, and add them to your list automatically. You still decide what to do. You just stop being the bottleneck for remembering. It's one of the jobs a good chief of staff has always done, and an AI chief of staff can now take on much of it.

## FAQ


**How do I keep track of follow-ups at work without a special tool?**


Use two lists in one place: what you owe and what you're waiting on. Write each item as who, what and when, capture it in the moment, and review both lists every week. A simple task app or spreadsheet is enough to start.


**How do I keep track of email follow-ups?**


Turn each email that needs a follow-up into a task with a date, rather than leaving it starred or unread. Many email apps also let you snooze messages or get a reminder if nobody replies. If most of your follow-ups live in email, an AI tool that reads your inbox can capture them automatically.


**How do I track follow-ups after a meeting?**


Read back every action item with an owner and a date before the meeting ends, then send a written recap. Add your own items to your "I owe" list and everyone else's to your "waiting on" list.


**How often should I follow up with someone?**


For most work requests, a polite check-in two to three working days after the expected date is reasonable. For urgent items, follow up sooner and say why it's time-sensitive.


**What's the best way for executives to track follow-ups?**


Executives make and receive so many commitments that manual tracking rarely keeps up. Many rely on a chief of staff or executive assistant (here's how those two roles differ), and more now use an AI tool like BOND to capture follow-ups from email, Slack and meetings automatically.


**What should a follow-up tracker include?**


At minimum: the task, the owner, the due or check-in date, where it came from (email, meeting, Slack) and its status. Keep it short enough that you'll actually update it.
